newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: No surprises seen from Malaysia's Tenaga results.
newsitem.headline: No surprises seen from Malaysia's Tenaga results.

text.p: Malaysian power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd is expected this week to report full-year net earnings of 1.0 billion to 1.2 billion ringgit ($397-$476 million), meeting market forecasts, analysts said.
They said they expect no surprises in the year ended August 31, with the stock likely to retain investors' favour after the government expressed support for the state-controlled power company.
A Tenaga official said the company will report its full-year results on Thursday.
The Estimate Directory of analysts' consensus put Tenaga's net earnings at an average of 1.13 billion ringgit, down 8.9 percent from 1.24 billion in 1995.

"The results should be operationally in line with last year's. But with lower foreign exchange gains, the net result should be lower than last year's," said Andrew Wong, power sector analyst at Schroder Research. Last year, Tenaga made a net profit of 213 million ringgit from foreign exchange gains.
Analysts said a boost to Tenaga's results would come from the one- to three-cent increase in electricity tariffs beginning from March 1.
This will add some 240 million ringgit to net earnings, said Phua Lee Kerk, an analyst at Vickers Ballas Research.

But the rate hike is offset by the continuing high cost of buying electricity from private power companies known as Independent Power Producers (IPPs), and some income loss and equipment damage caused by a 12 to 15 hour blackout over Peninsular Malaysia on August 3.
Tenaga has said it will give rebates totalling 70 million ringgit to all electricity consumers affected by the blackout.
Consumers living in northern Penang state will get an extra total of four million ringgit for a separate 10-day blackout on the island in June 1995.
Analysts said Tenaga will deduct the rebates from its bottom line in the next financial year.
The August blackout had led an embarrassed Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad to threaten to take away Tenaga's monopoly on transmission and distribution.
But things appear to have cooled down considerably since then.
The government, which has a 70 percent stake in Tenaga, made a series of announcements in the past two weeks that showed they were supporting the utility, analysts said.
Last week, Mahathir said Tenaga and not the private power companies, would get the bigger role in new electricity generation projects.
"The government has given Tenaga time to get its house in order. They are no longer emotional about it," said Lai Tak Heong, research director at Socgen-Crosby Research.

Responding to Tenaga complaints that its profits are being eroded by the prices it pays for electricity from IPPs, the government also said that IPPs would have to help bear the costs of supplying power to rural areas.
The improved perception has boosted Tenaga stock from a year-low close of 8.60 ringgit on October 4 to a close of 10.90 on Tuesday, a 27.5 percent surge within a month.
"Investors are trying to get back in (to Tenaga) after downgrading the stock," said an institutional salesman at a Malaysian brokerage.
($1 = 2.52 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
